title: "Policy"
---

This section will look at New York City, USA as a case study city, with their the [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf) strategy's goal to achieve "A Liveable Climate". Like most dense urban areas, New York City (NYC) is also facing the problems of warmer urban temperatures than its rural and suburban neighborhoods. Given growing events of higher frequency, longer lasting and more intense heat waves, this section will focus on one of NYC's experiencing climate threats of [Extreme Heat](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat).

## Summary

The OneNYC 2050: Building a Strong and Fair City is a long term strategic plan compromised of 8 goals and 30 initiatives. It frames its climate resilience goal under "A Livable Climate" recognising extreme heat as one of its major climate threats. Initiative 21 is directly relevant to the extreme heat challenge, envisioning community level interventions that aims to reduce vulnerability to climate impacts such as rising temperatures.

+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| A Livable Climate Obejectives, OneNYC 2050                                                                       |
+==================================================================================================================+
| 20. Achieve carbon neutrality and 100 percent clean electricity                                                  |
| 21. A LIVABLE CLIMATE Strengthen communities, buildings, infrastructure, and the waterfront to be more resilient |
| 22. Create economic opportunities for all New Yorkers through climate action                                     |
| 23. Fight for climate accountability and justice                                                                 |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Relevant Initiatives, Source: [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf)

OneNYC has stated extreme heat to be one of its "number one cause of mortality from weather conditions" ([OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf), p.32). Also known as the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, is a challenge that is widely faced by many cities globally. These neighborhoods tends to have concentrations dark surfaces from built structures, concrete and asphalt that absorbs and retain solar radiation throughout the day, while having limited green space to facilitate natural cooling through evapotranspiration and solar shading. The NYC has also identified limited access to air conditioning, energy costs and poor housing quality as drivers of such heat impacts ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)).

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![UHI, Source: [EARTH.ORG](https://earth.org/data_visualization/urban-heat-islands/)](images/w4_images/UHIfig1.jpg)
:::

"All heat deaths are preventable" ([Nyc.gov, 2019](https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/extreme-heat)). The OneNYC uses the Heat Vulnerability Index to identify neighborhoods that are more at risk following extreme heat. The risks are not evenly distributed across the city, where South Bronx, Central Brooklyn and Upper Manhattan are highlighted as the city's most heat vulnerable neighborhoods.

::: {layout-ncol="1"}
![HVI (Data Source: [EJNYC Full Data Explorer](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/6a3da7b920f248af961554bdf01d668b) )](images/w4_images/NYC_HVI_Map2.png)
:::

In action, the OneNYC strategy supports scientific based decision-making, and is commited to ensure that policies and physical actions are protective and cost effective. It is commited to intervene through a range of nature-based and built solutions, such as promoting urban forests efforts to combat extreme heat, installation of cool roofs to lower local temperatures and mitigate the health impacts from UHI as well as further green infrastructure investments.

## Application

### Data

Land surface temperature (LST) obtained from sensors are particularly useful for identifying the spatial pattern of surface heat across neighbourhoods and for monitoring how interventions change surface temperatures over time. The following datasets are commonly used for urban heat studies:

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Data                                                                                                                                                   | Benefits                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Limitations                                                                               |

| Landsat 8-9 Collection 2 Level 2 Operational Land Imager (OLI), Thematic Mapper (TM), Enhanced Thematic Mapper (ETM+), Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS)  | High spatial resolution, consistent data for long term monitoring                                                                                                                                                                 | Long revisit time of 8-16 days, unable to penetrate through clouds                        |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Terra and/or Aqua, MODIS                                                                                                                               | 36 bands LST measurement, global coverage with revisit time of every 1-2 days, allow large scale monitoring, phtosynthetic activity                                                                                               | Unable to penetrate through clouds (LST requires), coarse resolution                      |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| ECOSTRESS                                                                                                                                              | Highest spatial resolution thermal infrared space instrument, spatially continuous map of urban temperature, day and night coverage, able to monitor water vegetation stress responses and identify areas of at-risk 'hot spots'  | Unable to penetrate through clouds                                                        |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| LiDAR                                                                                                                                                  |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |                                                                                           |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Ground based temperature                                                                                                                               | Allow monitoring long term conditions of street level air temperature and humidity through studying of the urban boundary layer, which is the layer above the city where heat and moisture exchanges                              | Expensive for comprehensive coverage, locational biased installation may distort findings |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

: Source: [MODIS](https://terra.nasa.gov/about/terra-instruments/modis) , [Zhou et. al., 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/1/48) , [Solecki et.al., 2015](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nyas.12587) , [Hantson, 2013](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425712004610) ,

### Addressing Policy Challenge

For OneNYC’s “A Livable Climate” objective, remotely sensed evidence can support the following key objectives:

| Objectives | Application | Methodology | Remotely Sensing Data |
|----|----|----|----|
| Advance nature-based solutions to mitigate physical risks posed by climate change (e.g. urban forests) | Identify seasonal UHI trends to inform strategic planning and target areas that would benefit most from enhanced greenery systems to mitigate Urban Heat Island and Micro-Urban Heat Island (MUHI) developments. | Calculate LST from TIRS spectral bands 10 and 11 using NDVI, Land Surface Emissivity (LSE) and Brightness Temperature (BT), apply Machine Learning (ML) models (Random Forest, XGBoost) to predict LST reductions | Landsat 8-9 |
| Promote climate health preparedness for heat-vulnerable New Yorkers (e.g. cool roofs) | Understand and monitor spatialtemporal performances and trends of reflective coated cool roofs, to target areas for implementation | Band 10 satellite data with ML | Landsat 8-9 |
| Study emerging climate impacts to better understand NYC's built environment and communities | Identify locations of heat vulnerability - Heat Vulnerability Index; Surface Heat Assessment, | Obtain average surface temperature from remotely sensing data integrated with indicators (e.g. census); LST / LST prediction assessed through Universal Thermal Comfort Index (UTCI) and ML random forests classifer | LiDAR; ECOSSTRESS; Landsat 8-9 |
| Continue to refine the climate resiliency design guidelines | Not Applicable via Remote Sensing | \- | \- |

: Sources: [Ahmad, 2025](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394960889_Identifying_and_Combatting_Micro-Urban_Heat_Islands_in_New_York_City) , [Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) , [Boanni et.al., 2025](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sustainable-cities/articles/10.3389/frsc.2025.1655812/full) , [Environment & Health](https://a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov/IndicatorPublic/data-explorer/climate/?id=2411#display=summary) , [NYC Open Data](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Health/Heat-Vulnerability-Index-Rankings/4mhf-duep/about_data)

### Limitations and Integrated Approaches

Satellite thermal infrared data measures physical surface heat, not the street level air temperature humans actually experience, so it may overlook areas where extreme heat can cause deaths ([Shandas et.al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2225-1154/7/1/5), 2019). Integrating satellite data with ground-based measurements that is fairly distributed across the city can strengthen monitoring and improves accuracy, especially in neighbourhoods with higher heat vulnerability ([Mushore et.al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461) ; [Solecki et.al., 2015](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/nyas.12587)).

## Reflection

This section deepened my understanding of policy and remotely sensing data's role in addressing urban climate challenges. Remotely sensing data provides spatial evidence that bridges between policy objectives and decision-makings. This allowed translation of visionary strategies into actionable solutions.

Municipality policies tends to provide an overall vision for actions, governance and long-term goals, rather than technical implementation details. The OneNYC although did not detail in remotely sensing methods, but NYC works often involve tools that derives data from remotely sensing systems.

Many studies relied on satellite-based thermal infrared (TIR) data. A key insight is that it could be a limitation, as it captures purely surface temperature but not the temperature that humans experience at street level. This matters in dense neighborhoods where the urban form shapes heat exposure and health risk. This enables observations of variation of temperature across different land uses and land covers, providing a more throughout assessment of urban heat across the city. Critically, this method is more expensive and resource intensive for a large installation coverage.

This section also reinforced that data and visionary policies alone does not bring resilience. [Mushore et.al. (2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/15/23/5461)) have suggested the need of urban greening strategies to be scaled up to municipal level to be economically viable and effective. Without sustained investment and coordination across all boroughs as well as political support, OneNYC 2050's initiatives may remain a short fall otherwise.

On a global context, the goals and objectives aligns with international guidance such as UNEP’s Beat the Heat handbook on greening, cool surfaces, and planning, and it also connects to global goals through the SDGs, particularly SDG 3, SDG 11, and SDG 13 for "A Liveable Climate" ([UNEP, 2021](https://www.unep.org/resources/report/beating-heat-sustainable-cooling-handbook-cities) ; [OneNYC 2050](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/climate/downloads/pdfs/OneNYC_2050_Strategic_Plan.pdf)). Overall, OneNYC 2050 provides a positive, sustainable and ambitious strategy for addressing extreme heat, but its success depends on long term stakeholders collaboration and the technical and economic capacity needed to turn spatial evidence into equitable, actionable solutions.
